alt: Two panels. Rwanda: UNAMIR was present with a limited mandate, was reduced on 21 April 1994, and the genocide was ended by the RPF's victory in July 1994. Kosovo: NATO bombed from 24 March to 10 June 1999 without Security Council authorisation, followed by UN administration with KFOR. Below, four criteria for evaluating an intervention: lives saved, conflict ended, international law respected, justice delivered.
caption: Judge both cases by the same criteria.

alt: A vertical timeline: Belgian rule after 1918 hardened Hutu and Tutsi into racial categories on identity cards and favoured the Tutsi; Belgium later switched support to the Hutu; the Hutu revolution of 1959-1962 drove Tutsi into exile; the RPF invaded in October 1990; Hutu Power organised militias and radio propaganda; the Arusha Accords of August 1993 were seen as betrayal by extremists; and on 6 April 1994 the president's plane was shot down and killing began.
caption: Colonial categories, civil war and extremist organisation lay behind the genocide.

alt: Paired rows for 1994: Dallaire's January warning met an order not to raid arms caches; when killing began on 6-7 April, Belgium withdrew and Western states evacuated their nationals; on 21 April UNAMIR was reduced; as roughly 800,000 were killed in about a hundred days the US resisted the word genocide; France's Operation Turquoise began in June; and the RPF ended the genocide by taking Kigali in July.
caption: The outside world withdrew as the killing began; the RPF, not the UN, ended it.

alt: Two strands of impact. Refugees and regional war: around two million Hutu fled, many to camps in Zaire, and attacks from the camps contributed to the First Congo War of 1996-1997. International justice: the ICTR was created at Arusha in November 1994, and its 1998 Akayesu judgment was the first international conviction for genocide. In 1998 President Clinton acknowledged the international failure.
caption: The genocide spread war into Zaire and created new international justice.

alt: A vertical timeline: autonomy removed in 1989; non-violent resistance under Rugova; the Dayton Agreement of 1995 ignores Kosovo and the KLA begins attacks; Serbian offensives in 1998; Račak in January 1999; failed Rambouillet talks; NATO bombing from 24 March to 10 June 1999; Resolution 1244 placing Kosovo under UN administration; and Milošević indicted in May 1999, removed in 2000 and on trial from 2002.
caption: Non-violence, then insurgency, then NATO bombing and UN administration.

alt: A spectrum for Kosovo runs from humanitarian rescue and a valuable precedent to a breach of international law that weakened the UN, with the independent commission's verdict, illegal but legitimate, in the middle. For Rwanda, two cards: Samantha Power's argument that US officials chose not to act, and the continuing debate over France's role.
caption: Use these positions to frame Question 4 judgements.

alt: Origin, purpose and date of a UN force commander's memoir each lead to value or limitation. Origin: he took part in the decisions, a value. Purpose: to explain and justify himself and indict others, a limitation because he may stress others' faults. Date: nine years later, a value because of documents released since, and a limitation because memory may have been reshaped.
caption: Origin, purpose and date each point to value, limitation or both.
